sources.title: Inn-yard theatre
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It is an often-stated truism of the critical literature that the open-air public theatres or amphitheatres of Burbage and his successors were modeled on the inn yards, with their surrounding balconies, open space in the center, and stage to one side.

sources.title: Theatre (structure)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This layout is said to derive from the practice of holding plays in the yard of an inn.

sources.title: The Theatre
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The design of The Theatre was possibly adapted from the inn-yards that had served as playing spaces for actors and/or bear baiting pits.

views: From the inn yards: the usual account in the critical literature, 'an often-stated truism' (Inn-yard theatre); the layout 'is said to derive' from plays in an inn yard (Theatre (structure)).

Only possibly, or from the baiting rings: The Theatre's design was 'possibly adapted' from the inn yards 'and/or bear baiting pits' (The Theatre); the round baiting rings are the subject of the bear-garden link.

links.claim: The Bankside bear garden was a round or polygonal galleried ring like the playhouses beside it, and The Theatre may have been adapted from the baiting pits; in 1614 the Hope replaced the Bear Garden as a dual-purpose house for plays and baiting. The likeness and the replacement are documented; that the baiting ring shaped the playhouse is not shown.

sources.title: Beargarden
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Beargarden was constructed as a round or polygonal open structure, comparable to the public theatres built in and around London starting in 1576.

sources.title: Beargarden
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1613, Henslowe and new partner Jacob Meade tore down the Beargarden, and in 1614 replaced it with the Hope Theatre.

sources.title: Hope Theatre
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Also, the Hope was likely a more complex construction job, since it was designed as a dual-purpose facility from the start.

links.claim: Contemporaries called the London playhouses amphitheatres, and the Swan's columns were painted to give it a 'Roman' look; the sources show the name and the classical dress, not that the builders worked from Roman amphitheatres.

sources.title: The Swan (theatre)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Translated from the Latin, his description identifies the Swan as the "finest and biggest of the London amphitheatres", with a capacity for 3000 spectators.

sources.title: The Swan (theatre)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was built of flint concrete, and its wooden supporting columns were so cleverly painted that "they would deceive the most acute observer into thinking that they were marble", giving the Swan a "Roman" appearance.

sources.title: Amphitheatre
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Roman amphitheatres were circular or oval in plan, with a central arena surrounded by perimeter seating tiers.

links.claim: Some Cornish playing places reused older earthworks; Perran Round, the best surviving plen-an-gwary, is scheduled as a later Iron Age and early post-Roman enclosure (a round), while Henry Jenner thought it more probably built as a playing place.

sources.title: Perran Round
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It has been described as an Iron Age circular enclosure, or round and the citation under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Areas Act 1979 does describe Perran Round as a small enclosure of later Iron Age and early post-Roman period.

sources.title: Perran Round
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Henry Jenner compiled the scheduling paperwork which states that it is ″more probable″ that it was constructed as a plain-an-gwary, an open-air theatre for the performance of miracle plays although earlier structures were commonly repurposed as later 'playing places'.

views: A reused round: Perran Round is described as an Iron Age round, and the scheduling citation calls it an enclosure of the later Iron Age and early post-Roman period.
Built as a playing place: Henry Jenner's scheduling paperwork held it 'more probable' that it was constructed as a plain-an-gwary, while allowing that earlier structures were commonly repurposed.

links.claim: The Cockpit in Drury Lane was a cockfighting pit converted in 1616 into an indoor playhouse, perhaps to designs by Inigo Jones; Jones designed another 'Cockpit' theatre at Whitehall in 1629. One building's history, not the origin of every indoor playhouse (the Blackfriars was a hall).

sources.title: Cockpit Theatre
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The original building was an actual cockpit; that is, a staging area for cockfights.

sources.title: Cockpit Theatre
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In August 1616, Christopher Beeston acquired the lease to the building and converted it to an indoor playhouse.

links.claim: At the Restoration both patent companies briefly used the old indoor playhouses (the Cockpit, Salisbury Court) and quickly moved to new houses made from tennis courts; the Cockpit could not compete and no play is recorded there after 1665.

sources.title: Cockpit Theatre
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Both companies briefly made use of the earlier generation of theatres including the Cockpit and the Salisbury Court Theatre, but quickly moved to newer and more fashionable venues — Davenant in 1661 to a theatre in Lincoln's Inn Fields that was once Lisle's Tennis Court, and Killigrew in 1660 to Gibbon's Tennis Court in Vere Street.

links.claim: Killigrew and Davenant, following a French practice, turned real tennis courts into theatres: long, high galleried buildings of about the size of the earlier theatres. Lisle's Tennis Court (1656) became the first public playhouse in London with moveable scenery.

sources.title: Lisle's Tennis Court
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Taking a hint from their new King's taste, Killigrew and Davenant both chose a solution that had been used in France: converting tennis courts into theatres.

sources.title: Lisle's Tennis Court
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was originally an indoor tennis court; courts were used as theatre spaces because they had a similar structure with a narrow, rectangular shape and gallery seating.

sources.title: Lisle's Tennis Court
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The tennis court theatre was the first public playhouse in London to feature the moveable scenery that would become a standard feature of Restoration theatres.

links.claim: Inigo Jones, who learnt Italian set design, brought movable scenery and the proscenium arch to the English court masque; the Restoration playhouses put such scenery on the public stage, borrowing also from French opera.

sources.title: Inigo Jones
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Under the patronage of Queen Anne of Denmark (the consort of King James I), he is credited with introducing movable scenery and the proscenium arch to English theatre.

sources.title: Restoration spectacular
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The spectacular has roots in early 17th-century court masque, though it borrowed ideas and technology from French opera.

sources.title: Theatre (structure)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Italian opera houses were the model for the subsequent theaters throughout Europe.

links.claim: The Georgian Theatre Royal at Richmond (1788) keeps parts of the Restoration theatre layout (deep apron, proscenium doors, galleries). The source cites it as an example of that layout; it does not trace the line of development between them.

sources.title: Lisle's Tennis Court
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: However, a great example of the layout of the inside is the Georgian Theatre Royal in Richmond, North Yorkshire, which contains components of Restoration theatre spaces and still stands today.

links.claim: The music hall grew in the 1850s out of the saloons and song-and-supper rooms of the 1830s and 1840s (the Grecian Saloon, Evans's, the Coal Hole, the Mogul Saloon, on whose site the Middlesex was built).

sources.title: Music hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The music hall as we know it developed from such establishments during the 1850s and were built in and on the grounds of public houses.

sources.title: Music hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: According to John Hollingshead, proprietor of the Gaiety Theatre, London (originally the Strand Music Hall), this establishment was "the father and mother, the dry and wet nurse of the Music Hall".

links.claim: Music hall began in the saloon bars of pubs in the 1830s; in the 1850s some pubs were pulled down for music halls, and the Canterbury (1852), often counted the first, was built beside the Canterbury Tavern and looked like a pub concert room.

sources.title: Music hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Originating in saloon bars within pubs during the 1830s, music hall entertainment became increasingly popular with audiences—so much so, that during the 1850s some public houses were demolished, and specialised music hall theatres developed in their place.

sources.title: Music hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The hall looked like most contemporary pub concert rooms, but its replacement in 1854 was of then unprecedented size.

links.claim: From the 1880s music halls were rebuilt as larger variety theatres (the London Pavilion 1885, the Canterbury, Weston's as the Holborn Empire in 1906), and after 1918 the halls rebranded their shows as variety.

sources.title: Music hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: During 1906 it was rebuilt as a variety theatre and renamed as the Holborn Empire.

sources.title: Music hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It faded away after 1918 as the halls rebranded their entertainment as variety.

links.claim: Films were first shown in fairgrounds, music halls and converted shops; the Cinematograph Act 1909 set a building code for cinemas, the cinema took the halls' audience, and some halls became cinemas (Gatti's Hungerford Palace of Varieties in 1910).

sources.title: Cinematograph Act 1909
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: During the 1890s and 1900s, most film exhibition took place in temporary venues such as fairgrounds, music halls and hastily converted shops (so-called 'penny gaffs').

sources.title: Music hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The improvement of cinema, the development of radio, and the cheapening of the gramophone damaged its popularity greatly.

sources.title: Music hall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It became a cinema in 1910, and the Players' Theatre in 1946.

links.claim: The Romans made Bath a spa town; it revived as a spa in the Elizabethan era, and the 18th-century Pump Room and baths stand over the Roman spring.

sources.title: Bath, Somerset
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the 17th century, claims were made for the curative properties of water from the springs, and Bath became popular as a spa town in the Georgian era.

sources.title: Bath, Somerset
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The abbey church became derelict before being restored as the city's parish church in the Elizabethan era, when the city experienced a revival as a spa.

sources.title: Roman Baths (Bath)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The spring is now housed in 18th-century buildings, designed by architects John Wood, the Elder and John Wood, the Younger, father and son.

links.claim: The pump room is the spa's building, where the water was pumped up to be drunk; it was also the social room of the spa, as at Bath, where it formed one complex with the Lower Assembly Rooms.

sources.title: Pump rooms (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 71742)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A spa building to which water was pumped from springs or wells; usually also serving a social function as an ASSEMBLY ROOM, eg. as at Bath.

sources.title: Grand Pump Room
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Along with the Lower Assembly Rooms, it formed a complex where social activity was centred, and where visitors to the city gathered.

links.claim: The assembly rooms of the 18th and 19th centuries were in part supplanted by the ballrooms of the large hotels of the railway age.

sources.title: Assembly rooms
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Also to some extent they were supplanted by the ballrooms of major hotels as British hotels became larger from the railway age onwards.

links.claim: Structures for bands playing to guests were found in the 18th-century pleasure gardens of London (Vauxhall's orchestra); the Victorian park bandstand followed, the first in Britain in 1861, with the brass band movement.

sources.title: Bandstand
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: During the 18th and 19th centuries this type of performance building was found in the fashionable pleasure gardens of London and Paris where musicians played for guests dining and dancing.

sources.title: Bandstand
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Many bandstands in the United Kingdom originated in the Victorian era as the British brass band movement gained popularity.

links.claim: The seaside pier began as a landing stage for steamer passengers (Ryde, 1814) and became a promenade over the sea; working piers were later recycled as pleasure piers.

sources.title: Pier
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The large tidal ranges at many such resorts meant that passengers arriving by pleasure steamer could use a pier to disembark safely.

sources.title: Pier
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Following the building of the world's first seaside pier at Ryde, the pier became fashionable at seaside resorts in England and Wales during the Victorian era, peaking in the 1860s with 22 being built in that decade.

sources.title: Pier
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Many other working piers have been demolished, or remain derelict, but some have been recycled as pleasure piers.

links.claim: The racecourse grandstand (York, 1754) is the oldest kind of spectator stand; the football ground is a pitch with stands, the first purpose-built (Goodison Park, 1892) with stands on three sides, and a grandstand is in essence one section of a stadium. The sources give the parts and the order, not a line of descent.

sources.title: Grandstand (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69944)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: The principal stand at a sporting ground, eg. at a racecourse.

sources.title: Grandstand
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The grandstand is in essence like a single section of a stadium, but differs from a stadium in that it does not wrap all or most of the way around.

sources.title: Football ground (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 71809)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A site including a pitch, stands and other ancillary buildings associated with the game of football.
